package.description:
Smaller, slower meals that stop at comfortably full, and easier on greasy food, may ease tirzepatide (Mounjaro) nausea. On the label, stomach effects came mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time.

Get medical help right away for severe stomach pain that won't go away (it may spread to your back), with or without vomiting, or signs of a serious allergic reaction: 911 US/Canada, 999 UK, 000 Australia.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Watch next: tirzepatide's common side effects and how to manage them:

Mounjaro US PI, DailyMed (27 Aug 2026): https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=d2d7da5d-ad07-4228-955f-cf7e355c8cc0
CUH NHS dietitians (23 Apr 2026): https://www.cuh.nhs.uk/patient-information/dietary-advice-for-people-with-type-2-diabetes-using-tirzepatide-mounjaro/

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Nausea: Foods That May Help
script.hook_pattern: Drug-first direct question with the short answer in sentence 2 (by 15 s), a second payoff from the label's per-dose nausea rates at 15–30 s, then a one-sentence open loop (the NHS heartburn habit that isn't a food) paid off at about 66%, before the safety chapter

scenes.narration: On tirzepatide, or Mounjaro, which foods and habits may ease your nausea? Short answer: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping at comfortably full, and going easier on greasy food.

visual.stock_query: queasy woman at dinner table, hopeful

scenes.narration: Here's how common it is. On the Mounjaro label, in placebo-controlled trials of adults with type 2 diabetes, nausea affected 12 percent of people on 5 milligrams, 15 percent on 10, and 18 percent on 15. On placebo, it was 4 percent.

visual.stock_query: label document with nausea bar chart

scenes.narration: And the label adds the line people need to hear. Those stomach effects came mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time.
Stay with me, because the heartburn habit the NHS suggests isn't a food at all.
scenes.retention_device: One-sentence open loop (paid off in s42)

scenes.narration: Picture Priya, 49. She's hypothetical, but maybe familiar. A few days after her dose goes up, the dinner she's cooked a hundred times suddenly feels like a brick.

visual.stock_query: woman staring at full plate, uneasy

scenes.narration: She's hungry at six, queasy by seven, and quietly wondering if she's doing this wrong. If that's you, you're not failing. You're in the phase the label describes.

visual.stock_query: worried woman in kitchen at evening

scenes.narration: So why can a normal-size dinner suddenly feel like too much?

visual.stock_query: teal gradient chapter card, plate icon

scenes.narration: The Mounjaro label says tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. In plain English, food leaves your stomach more slowly than you're used to.
Here's the hopeful part. The label also says that delay is largest after the first dose and diminishes over time.

visual.myth: My stomach will always feel like this
visual.fact: Label: the delay is largest after the first dose and diminishes over time

scenes.narration: Think of a motorway with one lane closed. The traffic still gets through. It just can't all arrive at once.

Nobody can promise which tip will work for your stomach. But NHS dietitians and a joint advisory from four US lifestyle, nutrition and obesity societies point in the same direction. And it starts with size.
What can you actually do at dinner when nausea shows up?

visual.stock_query: teal gradient chapter card, fork icon

scenes.narration: First, size. An NHS dietitians' leaflet for people with type 2 diabetes on tirzepatide suggests small, frequent meals and avoiding large portions. The advisory also suggests smaller, more frequent meals.

Second, pace. Put your fork down between bites. The NHS leaflet suggests eating slowly and giving your food time to settle. Stopping when you're comfortably full might mean leaving food on the plate, and that's okay.

visual.stock_query: man resting fork between bites, calm

scenes.narration: Comfortably full may arrive earlier than it used to. Maybe at half the plate. That's not something to push through. It's a signal worth listening to.
Third, fat. Go easier on greasy, fried and very rich meals. The same NHS leaflet suggests avoiding very sweet, spicy, fatty or fried foods when you feel sick.
The joint advisory goes a step further. It suggests avoiding fatty or high-fibre foods during the first few days of treatment.

visual.stat_label: Advisory: avoid fatty or high-fibre foods early on

scenes.narration: Notice the scope. That's the first few days of treatment, not forever. Hold on to that, because fibre comes back as a hero in a few minutes.

visual.stock_query: oats bowl wearing a tiny cape

scenes.retention_device: New open loop (paid off in constipation chapter)

scenes.narration: Fourth, fluids. Small, regular sips through the day can feel easier than gulping a big glass with your meal.
And when you're queasy, plain, dry foods are an easy place to start: toast, crackers or plain biscuits.

visual.stock_query: plain toast and crackers on plate

scenes.narration: Back to Priya. She swaps to a smaller plate, eats more slowly, and saves the fried dish for later in the week. Small changes, all in the direction this guidance points.
But nausea isn't the only stomach effect on the label. Diarrhoea sits right next to it, and it brings its own question.

visual.stock_query: label page with next line highlighted

scenes.narration: What should you drink, and when does diarrhoea need attention?

visual.stock_query: teal gradient chapter card, water glass

scenes.narration: On the Mounjaro label, in the same trials of adults with type 2 diabetes, diarrhoea affected 12 to 17 percent of people across the 5 to 15 milligram doses. On placebo, it was 9 percent.
For diarrhoea, the NHS leaflet's advice is simple: stay well hydrated.

visual.stock_query: water jug and glass on table

scenes.narration: Know the signs. The NHS lists peeing less often than usual, dark yellow, strong-smelling pee, and feeling dizzy or tired.
Here's why that matters. The label carries a warning about kidney injury linked to fluid loss from vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration. Fluids aren't a nice extra. They matter.
scenes.retention_device: Stakes raised with a label warning

scenes.narration: And before you take any other medicine for diarrhoea, check with a pharmacist or doctor first.
Now, remember fibre, the food the advisory said to go easy on in the first few days of treatment? Here's where it switches sides.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to earlier loop, opens next chapter

scenes.narration: Can the same food be one to limit early on and a help later?
Constipation is on the Mounjaro label too. In adults with type 2 diabetes, it affected 6 to 7 percent of people across the 5 to 15 milligram doses, against 1 percent on placebo.

For constipation, the NHS leaflet suggests more fibre, like wholegrains, beans, fruit and vegetables, at least 2 litres of fluid a day, and moving more. Unless you've been told to limit fluids. Then follow your care team's advice.

items: At least 2 litres of fluid a day

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'fibre as hero' loop

scenes.narration: So which is it: less fibre, or more? The advisory's line covers the first few days of treatment. The NHS leaflet's advice is for constipation. If they seem to clash for you, a dietitian or your prescriber can help you balance them.

visual.myth: Fibre is always good, or always bad, on tirzepatide
visual.fact: Advisory: go easy on it in the first few days of treatment. NHS leaflet: more fibre for constipation

scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer, then resolution

scenes.narration: A practical middle path is to add fibre gradually, not all at once, and to pair it with fluids. And if diarrhoea is your main problem right now, hold off on extra fibre until it settles.
In Priya's week, the fried takeaway waits. But oats and berries are back at breakfast, a little at a time, with water alongside.
Which brings us to the evening, and the burning feeling that makes lying down a gamble.

visual.stock_query: man hesitating beside bed at night

scenes.narration: What helps heartburn and burping on tirzepatide?
The Mounjaro label lists burping, reflux and bloating among the stomach effects reported more often than on placebo.
Indigestion is in the label's main table too: 5 to 8 percent across the doses, against 3 percent on placebo, in adults with type 2 diabetes.
The NHS heartburn advice starts with ideas you'll recognise: eat smaller, more frequent meals, and avoid the foods and drinks that trigger your symptoms.

visual.stock_query: small plates spread through the day

scenes.narration: It also suggests skipping clothes that are tight around your waist. Small, but easy to try.
And here's the habit I promised, the one that isn't a food. The NHS suggests not eating within 3 to 4 hours of going to bed.

visual.stat_label: NHS heartburn advice: no eating before bed
visual.stock_query: clock and empty plate at night

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: It also suggests raising the head end of your bed by 10 to 20 centimetres, so your chest and head sit above your waist.

visual.stock_query: bed head raised on blocks, night room

scenes.narration: For Priya, that means dinner a little earlier, and the late-night snack moves to the afternoon. Not a diet rule. Just timing.

visual.stock_query: woman eating early dinner, sunset window

scenes.narration: For burping, two easy things to test: eat more slowly, and go easier on fizzy drinks.
But eating less raises a different question. Are you still getting what your body needs?

visual.stock_query: thoughtful man looking at small plate

scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before section change

scenes.narration: When portions shrink, what deserves the first spot on your plate?

visual.stock_query: teal gradient chapter card, egg icon

scenes.narration: The joint advisory stresses getting enough protein and nutrient-dense foods while appetite is lower, partly to help protect muscle.
One simple approach is to start the meal with the protein: eggs, yoghurt, fish, beans, tofu or chicken. Then the rest of the plate, if there's room.
One important exception: if you have kidney disease, check with your prescriber or a dietitian before raising your protein. The right amount isn't the same for everyone.
And if you have diabetes, eating much less matters in another way. The label says the risk of low blood sugar is higher when tirzepatide is used with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
If that's you, and nausea means you're eating far less than usual, tell your prescriber. Don't wait for it to sort itself out.
Now, one label warning almost nobody hears about involves your stomach and an operating room.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop, paid off next scene

scenes.narration: The label warns about a risk of breathing stomach contents into the lungs during general anaesthesia or deep sedation. Before any planned surgery or procedure, tell your healthcare team you take tirzepatide.
So when is a rough stomach more than a rough week?
Call your prescriber if vomiting or diarrhoea won't settle, if you can't keep fluids down, or if you notice those signs of dehydration.
The label also carries a gallbladder warning. So new or unusual belly pain is worth a call too, not something to sit on.

Get medical help right away if you have severe stomach pain that won't go away, which may spread to your back, with or without vomiting. The same goes for signs of a serious allergic reaction, like swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing.

items: Severe stomach pain that won't go away
Swelling of face, lips, tongue, throat

scenes.narration: For those, call 911 in the US or Canada, 999 in the UK, or triple zero in Australia.
scenes.retention_device: Help lines for all four markets

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
Not personal advice: talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether tirzepatide is right for you.
So, what happened to Priya's dinners?

A few weeks on, in our hypothetical, the plate is smaller, dinner's earlier, and the queasy evenings come less often. That matches the label's pattern: mostly during dose escalation, decreasing over time.
scenes.retention_device: Emotional payoff tied to the label

scenes.narration: If you keep three things: smaller, slower meals that stop at comfortably full. Easier on greasy food, with fluids through the day. And a call to your prescriber when it won't settle.
And if this phase has left you frustrated or worried, that's understandable. It isn't a willpower test. It's a phase the label itself describes.
If this helped, subscribe for calm, evidence-first tirzepatide videos that answer the questions you actually search. There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.
scenes.retention_device: Single subscribe ask after the payoff, watch-next close (post notes: watch-next target = Side Effects video; publisher adds its verified URL, never a placeholder or channel home)

factcheck.summary: The script is accurate and safe. It passes with five small fixes. I checked every number against the live DailyMed Mounjaro label. These all match Table 1: nausea 4/12/15/18%, diarrhoea 9/12/13/17%, constipation 1/6/6/7% and indigestion 3/8/8/5%. Burping, reflux and bloating all appear in the label's list of extra stomach effects reported more often than on placebo. The script's population (adults with type 2 diabetes, placebo-controlled) is correct. Three label lines are quoted correctly: stomach effects mostly during dose escalation and decreasing over time, the slower stomach emptying being 'largest after the first dose and diminishes over time', and the kidney injury, aspiration, gallbladder and low blood sugar warnings. The low blood sugar line is correctly limited to people with diabetes on insulin or a sulfonylurea. The Cambridge NHS dietitians' leaflet (approved 23 Apr 2026) supports the advice on small frequent meals, avoiding large portions, eating slowly, plain dry foods, avoiding sweet, spicy, fatty or fried food, the constipation advice (fibre, beans and pulses, at least 2 litres of fluid, more activity) and the 'comfortably full' idea. The joint advisory's sentence matches word for word: 'Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms.' The NHS heartburn page (3 or 4 hours before bed, 10–20 cm, tight waistbands, smaller meals, trigger foods) and the NHS dehydration signs also match. Priya is clearly labelled as hypothetical, and nothing about her is shaming. The safety lines follow the house rules: the emergency triggers with 'right away', help lines for all four markets, the scoped don't-stop line and the prescriber line. The minor fixes: (1) a fibre caveat for people who have diarrhoea, (2) a caveat for people told to limit fluids on the 2-litre tip, (3) a source tag in s56, (4) softer on-screen wording in s27, and (5) correcting where S6 was co-published. One limit on my check: Lilly's Zepbound PDF (S2) opened but its text couldn't be read. Every line tagged S2 is also confirmed by S1.

issues.claim: A practical middle path is to add fibre gradually, not all at once, and to pair it with fluids.
issues.problem: The video moves straight from the diarrhoea chapter into 'fibre switches sides' and 'add fibre'. A viewer who has diarrhoea could take this as a cue to eat more fibre. The leaflet's fibre advice is for constipation, and one reading of its diarrhoea section advises avoiding high-fibre foods. Two fetches of the page gave different results on this, so the fix below is our own caution, untagged, and doesn't quote the leaflet.
issues.fix: Narration: "A practical middle path is to add fibre gradually, not all at once, and to pair it with fluids. And if diarrhoea is your main problem right now, hold off on extra fibre until it settles." (No source tag.)

issues.claim: at least 2 litres of fluid a day
issues.problem: The source is correct, but the tip has no caveat for people who have been told to limit fluids (for example, some people with heart failure or advanced kidney disease).
issues.fix: Add to the end of the s32 narration: "Unless you've been told to limit fluids. Then follow your care team's advice."

issues.claim: Call your prescriber if vomiting or diarrhoea won't settle… — tagged S5, S7
issues.problem: The NHS tirzepatide page (S7) only says to speak to a pharmacist or doctor about side effects that bother you or don't go away. The more specific 'if your diarrhoea does not settle, speak to your doctor' comes from the Cambridge leaflet (S3), which isn't tagged.
This is stronger than the label. The label warns about kidney injury linked to fluid loss; it doesn't say fluids protect your kidneys. The on-screen text shouldn't be stronger than the narration.

issues.claim: Obesity Pillars (co-published with Am J Clin Nutr), PMC full text
issues.problem: The publisher field is incomplete. The PMC record is the Obesity Pillars version, and the advisory was co-published in more than one journal.
issues.fix: publisher: "Obesity Pillars (joint advisory; also co-published elsewhere), PMC full text". Keep the year as 2025.

thumbnail.reasoning: Candidate #0 directly repeats the title's own words ("Which Foods Help?" mirrors "What Foods May Help?"), triggering the repetition cap (CTR ≤5) even though it's legible and has a decent character reaction. Candidate #1 ("IT'S HOW YOU EAT?") keeps a genuine curiosity gap and doesn't give away the answer, but the headline is broken into three short, choppy lines which hurts instant legibility at phone size, and it pivots away from the title's explicit promise of "foods," risking a mild bait-and-switch feel. Candidate #2 ("QUEASY AFTER MEALS?") has the strongest single-line, large-type legibility, a clean high-contrast before/after visual with one clear focal transformation, doesn't give away the answer or repeat the title's wording, and stays squarely on-topic with the nausea/food-help premise — making it the strongest, most honest click driver with the best phone-size readability.
